activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: On a clear, sunny day, the sky looks blue.
story:
Axel sat at the big table. He wanted to paint a picture of the sky. He picked up a gray crayon first. He drew a big gray sky. Then he looked out the window.

The sun was shining. The sky outside was not gray. The sky was blue. "Mama, look!" said Axel. "The sky is blue today." Mama smiled and nodded. Axel put the gray crayon down. He picked up the blue crayon instead. He drew a new blue sky. It looked just like the real one.

Then Axel wanted to build the rest of his picture. He painted a yellow sun in the corner. He painted green grass at the bottom. He painted a red ball on the grass. Every part was a different color.

Mama hung the picture on the wall. Axel stood back and looked at it. "Blue sky, sunny day," he said softly. Mama clapped her hands. Axel clapped too.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: On a traffic light, red means stop and green means go.
story:
Chloe went to the store with Grandma. She wanted a red balloon. The store was out of red ones. "We can look again next week," said Grandma. Chloe held Grandma's hand. A big pig statue stood by the door. It was too heavy to move. Chloe patted its nose.

Outside, they waited at the street. A tall light hung over the road. It turned red. All the cars stopped. "Red means stop," said Chloe. The light turned green. The cars all went. "Green means go!" she called.

Back home, Chloe found a yellow crayon. She drew the tall light. She drew a green one, and cars going. She drew a red one, and cars stopping. Then she drew a blue sky over it all. Chloe hung her picture by the door. "Now we can practice," she said.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: A small pet like a guinea pig is held gently with two hands while sitting down, so it cannot fall far.
story:
Nathan went to the park with his dad. They were bringing home a baby guinea pig. Nathan wanted to carry her around. He held her with one hand and stood up tall.

"Sit down on the grass," said Dad. "Hold her with two hands." Nathan sat down. He cupped his two hands under her. The guinea pig felt warm and soft.

Nathan tried to stand. She wiggled. Nathan sat right back down. "Two hands, sitting down," said Dad. Nathan held her with two hands, sitting down. The guinea pig made a little squeak. That was the surprise. She licked his thumb.

"She likes me," said Nathan. Dad smiled. At home, Nathan helped clean her bowl. He held her again, with two hands, sitting down on the floor.

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
fact: Holding the paper still with your other hand helps keep it from sliding.
story:
Charles sat at the little table at school. He had a big yellow pencil. He wanted to write his name all by himself. "C for Charles!" he said.

He pressed down the pencil. Then his paper slipped away. His C went wiggly and long. "Oh no!" said Charles. His teacher came over. "Try your other hand," she said. Charles put his other hand flat on the paper. He held it still.

Now he drew the C. The paper did not slip. The C was round and neat. Then he made an H, an A, and more letters. He wrote C-H-A-R-L-E-S! Charles jumped up. He ran to show his friend. "Look! I wrote my whole name!" he said. His friend clapped and clapped.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: A leash clipped to a dog's collar keeps the dog close to the person walking it.
story:
Elijah sat in a small room at the vet. A puppy sat in a box beside him. The puppy was tiny and brown. "Is he mine now?" Elijah asked. "Yes," said Mom. "He is your first pet."

The vet smiled. She clipped a leash to the puppy's collar. "There," she said. "The leash." Elijah held the leash with both hands. It felt smooth and long.

Then a bird flew by the door. The puppy wanted to chase it. He pulled and pulled. But the leash was clipped to his collar. And Elijah held on tight. So the puppy stayed close to Elijah. "Look, Mom!" said Elijah. "The leash keeps him close to me!"

At home, the puppy's tummy made a little growl. "Is he hungry?" Elijah wondered. Mom said yes. Elijah filled the bowl. The puppy ate it all up. Then he got sleepy, not grumpy at all. He curled up on his blanket.

"Can we walk him tomorrow?" Elijah asked. Mom laughed. "Yes. And you can hold the leash." Elijah patted the puppy's soft head. "Good night, puppy," he whispered.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Families often gather together to celebrate special holidays.
story:
Rosalie went to Grandma's house. Lots of cars sat outside. "Why so many cars?" she asked. Grandma smiled. "It is a special holiday. Families gather together to celebrate." Rosalie looked and looked. Aunties and uncles walked in the door. Then came her cousin Leo! She had not seen Leo for a long, long time. "Leo!" she called. They hugged and jumped.

Inside, Grandma set out little clay lamps. Grandma lit them with a match. Rosalie watched from far away. The lamps made the room glow.

"Look," said Rosalie. "The lamps are round like a wheel." Grandma laughed. "Yes, little and round."

Rosalie held Leo's hand. They walked past the lamps together.

"More lamps, more light," said Rosalie. Leo clapped.

activity: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
knowledge_domain: polite and functional phrases such as please, thank you, sorry and asking for help
fact: Saying 'excuse me' is a polite way to get past someone who is in your way.
story:
Austin went to the store with Mama. He wanted the big orange carrot on the shelf. The carrot looked like a rocket ship. "Zoom, zoom," said Austin.

But a lady with a cart stood in the way. Austin tried to squeeze past. His tummy bumped the cart. "Oops," said Austin. "Sorry, cart!"

Mama bent down. "Say excuse me," she said. "Excuse me," said Austin. The lady smiled and moved her cart. The aisle was open! Austin walked right through.

He reached up on tiptoe. The carrot was too high. "Please, help," said Austin. Mama handed him the carrot. "Thank you," said Austin.

At home, Mama cut the carrot for snack. Austin took a crunchy bite. Then he put the frozen peas in his toy cart. "Excuse me," he told the cat. The cat moved one paw. Austin rolled his cart past, all the way to the moon.

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: People often wear special clothes to a celebration.
story: Today was the big festival at home. Madeline ran to her drawer. She held up her old play shorts. She held up her red dress with gold flowers. Daddy came in. He wore his long white shirt with shiny buttons. Mommy wore her silk sari that went swish, swish. "We wear special clothes today," Daddy did say. So Madeline put on the red dress. It twirled when she spun. Downstairs, Grandma was lighting the lamps. Grandma let Madeline watch from far away. The little flames made the room glow. Madeline spun again and her dress caught the light. "Look at me!" she said. Outside the sky looked stormy and gray. But inside, the lamps and the gold flowers shone. Grandma smiled and clapped. Then Madeline saw her loose tooth wiggle in the mirror. She laughed a big laugh, and the dress twirled one more time.

activity: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
knowledge_domain: basic time concepts such as yesterday, today, tomorrow, now and later
fact: Yesterday is the day before today.
story:
Sophia sat at the dinner table. The lamp glowed soft and yellow. Daddy set down three bowls of soup. "Now we eat," said Daddy. Sophia spooned up one bite, two bites, three bites.

"I went to the park tomorrow," said Sophia.

Daddy looked up. "Tomorrow?" he asked. "Tomorrow is the day that comes next."

Sophia shook her head. "No. I already went. I went yesterday." Yesterday was the day before today. Yesterday she had slid down the big slide. Yesterday was all done.

"Mmm, yesterday you went to the park," said Daddy. "Today we eat soup. Tomorrow we can go again."

"Tomorrow," said Sophia. She held up one finger. "One more sleep?"

"One more sleep," said Daddy. "Now we eat. Later we wash our messy faces."

Sophia ate one more bite, then two. "Now it is later," she said. Her face was messy with soup.

Daddy laughed. He wiped her cheek with a soft cloth. "Now it is clean," he said.

Sophia looked at her bowl. All gone. "Tomorrow, park," she said. "After one more sleep."

"Yes," said Daddy. "One more sleep, and then the slide."

activity: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
knowledge_domain: to name the primary colours and mix two of them to make a new colour
fact: Adding white paint to a colour makes it lighter.
story:
Olivia sat at the wooden table. She had red paint, yellow paint and blue paint. Mama had a question for her. "Can you paint a sunny day?" Olivia nodded fast. A sunny day! She could not wait.

She painted the sun first. Red and yellow made orange when she stirred them. "Orange like a pumpkin!" she said. Then she painted the sky blue. Big swipes of blue all across the paper.

Olivia held up her paper. She frowned. The sky was too dark. It did not look like morning at all. It looked like night. She wanted a light, bright sky. She almost cried, but she did not.

Then she saw the white paint pot. She scooped some white with her brush. She stirred it into the blue. Round and round she stirred. She stopped and looked. The blue was lighter now! It was a soft morning blue. Olivia gasped. White paint made the blue lighter!

She painted a big light sky. Then she painted green grass. She mixed yellow and blue in a cup. Round and round. Green! Olivia held up her paper high. "Look, Mama! Sun, sky, grass!" Mama clapped. "What a sunny day," said Mama. Olivia dipped her brush again. "Now I will paint pink flowers!"

activity: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
knowledge_domain: the rote number words from one to ten heard in counting songs and everyday counting
fact: A number word always means the same amount: 'three' always means three things.
story:
Mya was in the playroom. She wanted to build a tower. Her brother Sam had the blocks. "Can I have three blocks?" she asked.

Sam gave her one big block. Then he gave her two little blocks. Mya looked at her pile. "That is only one big one," she said. "I want three."

Sam counted with her. "One, two, three," he said, tapping each block. "Three blocks. Big or little, three is three." Mya tapped them too. One, two, three. Three blocks, just like Sam said. She felt lucky to have such a nice brother.

Now she had her blocks. But she wanted more. "Can I have five?" she asked. Sam gave her five little blocks. Mya counted them out loud. "One, two, three, four, five." Five blocks. It worked again!

Mya stacked her blocks up high. "Ten blocks in my tower," she said. She counted them from the bottom. "One, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten." The tower stood tall. Then it wobbled. "Oops," said Mya. Sam laughed and held it steady. "Good job," he said. Mya put one more block on top, very slowly.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: You can pretend to take care of a doll or stuffed animal, like feeding it or tucking it into bed.
story:
Blake's teddy, Brown, felt hot. He was sick, and he would not smile.

"I will be your doctor," Blake said. She held a spoon of pretend medicine to his mouth. "Drink this." Brown drank it all up. Then Blake got her old blanket. She tucked Brown into bed, just like Mama does for her. She patted his head. "Sleep now, little bear."

Brown slept for a long time. Blake waited. Then Brown blinked his eyes. Blake gave him a pretend sandwich and a pretend cup of tea. "Eat and grow strong," she said. Brown grew strong. He jumped out of bed and danced on the rug.

"My job is done," said Doctor Blake. She put her toys in a neat row. Brown sat on the pillow and waved his paw. "Same time tomorrow," Blake whispered.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Loud and quiet are opposites.
story:
Jacob ran to the playground. He ran fast. His baby sister Lily went slow. She rode in her wagon.

Jacob saw a big slide and a small slide. He took the big one. The sun felt hot. Lily's juice box was cold. She drank it all up.

Then it was naptime for Lily. She laid in the wagon under a tree. But Ben was there. Ben banged his drum. He banged it loud. Lily woke up and cried.

"Can you make it quiet?" Jacob asked.

"Loud and quiet are opposites," said Ben. "Watch this."

Ben tapped the drum. Tap, tap, tap. So quiet. So soft. Lily closed her eyes. She fell asleep.

"Shh," said Jacob. He gave Ben a pretend gift, a big green leaf.

"Ooh," said Ben. "Is it smelly?"

"It's a grassy smell," said Jacob.

They giggled, very, very quietly.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: Feelings change, so a sad feeling can turn into a happy one later.
story:
Jake ran to the window at school. It was raining. Big drops went tap, tap, tap.

"No park today," said his friend Mia. Her face looked sad. Her mouth turned down.

Jake felt sad too. He wanted the swings. He wanted the slide.

Then Miss Lily clapped her hands. "We can build a fort inside!" she said.

Jake felt excited. His tummy went flutter, flutter. He got a clean blanket from the shelf. Mia got another one. They put the blankets over two chairs. It made a little house.

"Come in," said Jake. Mia crawled inside. It was soft and warm. It smelled like soap and grandma's hugs.

"My turn to spell a word," said Mia. She spelled C-A-T on the fort wall with her finger.

Jake laughed. His sad feeling was gone. Now he felt happy.

"See," said Mia, smiling wide. "I'm happy now."

Jake smiled back and pulled the blanket snug.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
fact: A grown-up helps a child sign up for a first library card.
story:
Edouard loved the bookmobile. It was a little truck full of books. It came to his street every Tuesday.

Edouard ran to the steps. He saw his friend Pia show a small card. The man at the desk scanned it. Then Pia took a book home.

"I want a card too," said Edouard. "Can I get one today?"

He tried to sign up all by himself. The man shook his head. "A grown-up helps a child sign up for a first library card," he said.

Edouard looked around. There was Grandma, waiting by the steps. He begged her, "Please come with me!"

Grandma followed him to the desk. She wrote her name. Edouard wrote his own name too. His letters wiggled like little worms. The man smiled and gave him a shiny new card.

Edouard picked a book about diggers. He held the card up high. "Look what my name did!" he said. Grandma laughed as the digger book fell open in his hands.

activity: searching for a lost favorite toy
knowledge_domain: searching for a lost favorite toy
fact: A lost and found is a place where people put things they find, so the owners can get them back.
story:
Sara ran to the park with her bunny. She hugged him tight. "We will play all day!" she said.

Then Sara saw the swings. She ran so fast. She pumped her legs. She went up high. But when she jumped off, her hands were empty. Her bunny was gone!

Sara looked in the sandbox. One, two, three scoops. No bunny. A dog barked at her. "Woof, woof!" Sara looked behind the bench. She looked by the water cup fountain. Still no bunny.

A park lady with a thin red scarf came over. "Try the lost and found," she said. "People put things they find there. Then the owners can get them back."

Sara ran to the little green box. She opened the lid. One mitten. One hat. One bunny!

"Bunny!" Sara shouted. She hugged him soft and warm. "Now we swing together." And she held him tight, up and up, all the way home.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Open and closed are opposites, like a door that is open or shut.
story:
Mia was thirsty after helping Mama shop. She wanted cold milk. The big fridge was closed. "Closed means shut tight," said Mama. Mia pulled the door. Now it was open! She got her small cup. She drank the milk fast, like a bunny. Then she put the cup down slow, like a turtle.

Mama was at the stove. The stove was hot, so Mama held the pan. Mia stayed far away. "Is the fridge open or shut?" Mama asked. Mia looked. The door was open. Could the door be open and shut? No, it was one or the other. Open and shut were opposites, Mama said.

Mia pushed the door. Click. It was shut now. "I closed it!" she said. The fridge hummed its happy hum. One door, shut tight. "Good job," said Mama. "Do you want warm oatmeal too?" Mia nodded and watched the pot bubble.

activity: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
knowledge_domain: basic color words such as red, blue, yellow and green
fact: You see colors with your eyes; you cannot tell a color by feeling it with your fingers.
story:
At school, Miss Dana held up a big cloth bag. "It is a feely bag," she said. "You put your hand in. You touch. You guess." Scarlett wanted to go first. It was her favorite game.

Scarlett put her hand in the bag. The thing inside felt round and smooth. "A ball!" she said. She rolled it in her fingers. Then she shouted, "A red ball!" Miss Dana smiled. "Now pull it out and look." Scarlett pulled it out. The ball was blue! Everyone laughed, even Scarlett. "My fingers told me it was a ball," she said. "My fingers did not tell me the color."

Next came Ben. He patted the bag. He felt something soft. "A sock! Is it green?" He pulled it out. The sock was yellow. "Close try," said Scarlett. "You must use your eyes for colors."

Then Scarlett felt again. Something small and bumpy. "Is it a crayon?" she asked. Miss Dana nodded. "What color do you see?" Scarlett looked. The crayon was green, her favorite color. On the wall, Miss Dana pointed to a sign with green on it. "Green like the grass," said Scarlett. "I saw it with my eyes!"

activity: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
knowledge_domain: welcoming a new baby brother or sister into the family
fact: Big brothers and sisters can help by fetching things, like a clean diaper.
story:
Zoe rode in the car with Daddy. The road was long and the sky was cloudy. "We are going to meet the baby," said Daddy.

At the hospital, Mommy sat in a big bed. A tiny baby was in her arms. "This is your new brother," said Mommy. Zoe looked at the baby. He was so small. Everyone looked at the baby. Nobody looked at Zoe. She wanted to hide under the chair.

Then the baby made a little cry. "Oh," said Mommy. "He needs a clean diaper." Daddy looked in the bag. He could not find it. "Zoe, can you help?" he asked. "Big sisters can fetch things."

Zoe ran to the bag. She found the clean diaper. She brought it to Daddy. "Thank you, Zoe," said Mommy. "Now can you find a soft blanket?"

Zoe found a blue blanket. She carried it to the bed. Daddy put the diaper on the baby. Then he wrapped the baby in the blanket. The baby stopped crying. He opened his little eyes.

"Sit here," said Mommy. Zoe sat next to her. Mommy laid the baby in Zoe's arms. Zoe held him very softly. "Hello, baby," said Zoe. The baby held her finger.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: Asking "Are you okay?" shows someone you care about how they feel.
story:
Elena stood by her bedroom window. It was windy outside. The tree waved its leaves. On her table was a little toy pond with a small duck floating on it.

Elena wanted the duck. She reached up on her toes. Her teddy bear sat on the edge of the table. Oops. The teddy fell down. He landed on the floor, face down.

Elena felt scared. She ran over. She picked teddy up. His head drooped. He looked sad. Elena patted his soft ears. Then she held him close and asked, "Are you okay?"

Teddy did not answer. But Elena asked again, soft and slow. "Are you okay, teddy?" She gave him a hug. His head popped up. Now he looked happy again. Elena smiled a big smile. She felt excited.

"Mama!" she called. "I asked teddy if he was okay!" Mama came in. "That was kind," said Mama. Elena sat teddy on the pillow. She kissed his nose.

Then Elena pointed at the duck. "Can I send the duck across the pond?" Mama blew on the water, gently. The duck sailed to the other side.

Elena clapped her hands. "Again!" she said.

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
fact: Practicing your name many times makes the letters easier to write.
story:
Mason was at Grandpa's house. He wanted to write his name all by himself. Grandpa gave him a big pencil. "Hold it like this," Grandpa said. He turned the pencil in Mason's small hand. The cat sat on the table to watch.

Mason tried the letter M. It came out wiggly. "Why is it so hard?" he asked. "Try it again and see," said Grandpa. So Mason wrote M, then M, then M. Each M looked better. "M, A, S, O, N," he said, naming the letters. He wrote his whole name. Then he wrote it again. The letters came out neat.

The next day, Mason wrote his name again. It was easy now. He was not afraid of the big M anymore. "Look, Grandpa! I did it five times!" Grandpa laughed. "Put it on the fridge," he said. Mason clapped his hands and picked up the pencil one more time.

activity: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
knowledge_domain: basic emotions such as happy, sad, angry, scared and excited
fact: Saying how you feel, like "I feel sad," helps grown-ups know how to help you.
story: Owen got to the playground early. The sun felt warm on his face. He wanted to go on the big red swing. But a big kid was on it. Owen waited and waited. He sat on a bench with his little pillow from the car. He did not say anything. He just frowned. Dad looked at him. Dad did not know what was wrong. Then Owen said, "I feel sad. I want the red swing." Dad smiled. "Now I can help you," Dad said. Dad asked the big kid to take turns. The big kid said yes! Owen clapped his hands. The swing went up high. The wind whooshed past his ears. "I feel happy!" Owen shouted. Dad laughed and gave him a big push.

activity: learning to swim at the local pool
knowledge_domain: learning to swim at the local pool
fact: Many pools ask swimmers to take a shower before getting in.
story:
Matteo ran to the pool with his dad. "Swim! Swim!" he shouted. He was so excited. He wanted to jump in right now.

A lady by the door held up her hand. "Wait," she said. "Shower first." Matteo stopped. He looked up at his dad.

"Many pools ask swimmers to take a shower before getting in," Dad said. "Come on. The showers are here."

Matteo stood under the little shower. Warm water ran down his arms. His thick hair got all wet and shiny. He laughed. He shook like a puppy. Water went everywhere!

Then Matteo ran to the pool steps. He stepped in slowly. The water did not feel cold at all. "Warm!" he said. He held Dad's hand and kicked his legs. Splash, splash.

A girl next to him was shivering. She had skipped the shower. "Brrr," she said. Matteo saw that she was cold. "Shower first," he told her. "Shower first!"

The girl ran to the showers. She came back with wet, shiny hair too. "Better!" she said. She smiled at Matteo.

Matteo kicked his legs again. Splash, splash, splash. Dad clapped. "You are swimming, Matteo!"

Matteo looked at the showers. "Shower first," he said. "Then swim!"

activity: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
knowledge_domain: common daily routines such as eating, sleeping, bathing and getting dressed
fact: Brushing or combing your hair gets the tangles out.
story:
Layla woke up in her big girl bed. Her heart was happy. Today she would wear her new dress.

She jumped out of bed. She ran to her mirror. "Oh no," said Layla. Her hair looked like a bird's nest. It was all puffy and wild.

"I can't wear my dress like this," she said. She found her brush on the shelf. She touched her hair. There were little knots in it. She pulled the brush fast. "Ow!" she said. That hurt.

Layla thought for a minute. She tried again. She brushed slowly, one small bit at a time. The knots came out, one by one. Soon her hair was smooth and shiny. "It worked!" she said.

Mama came in with her yellow dress. "You brushed your own hair," said Mama. "May I ask how it got so pretty?" "I brushed it slow," said Layla. "The slow way wins."

After her bath that night, Mama helped her put on pajamas. Layla was tired but still awake. She put the brush by her bed. "For my morning nest," she said. She patted her smooth hair and closed her eyes.

activity: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
knowledge_domain: basic social rules such as turn-taking, sharing, fairness and following simple group rules
fact: When someone is sleeping, we use a quiet voice.
story:
Evan ran to the sandbox. He wanted to dig a big hole. His friend Mia wanted to dig it too. "My turn first," said Evan. "Then my turn," said Mia. The teacher said, "Yes, take turns." Evan dug one scoop. Then Mia dug one scoop. The hole grew and grew.

Then the teacher brought in a little basket. In the basket was a baby. The baby was sleeping. It was the teacher's baby, and it came on the last day of the week. Evan looked at the baby. The baby's eyes were shut tight. How quiet a sleeping baby looks, he thought. Where do babies go when they sleep?

Ben ran up to the sandbox. "LOOK AT MY BIG STICK!" he shouted. The baby moved. The baby began to cry. The teacher picked the baby up. She patted its back, very soft. "Shh," she said. "When someone is sleeping, we use a quiet voice." Evan looked at Ben. Ben looked at Evan. Then Ben held up his stick again. "Look at my stick," he whispered. The baby stopped crying. The baby went back to sleep.

Evan whispered to Mia, "Your turn now." Mia dug the hole, one soft scoop. Evan watched the sleeping baby. He put one finger on his lips. "Shh," he whispered, and smiled.

activity: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
knowledge_domain: opposite pairs such as big and small, hot and cold, fast and slow
fact: Up and down are opposites.
story:
Wyatt wants to go down the big slide at school. But the slide is tall. His feet feel small on the ground. He runs to his friend Mia. "Watch me," Mia says. She climbs up the ladder. Up, up, up she goes. Then she slides down, down, down. "Up and down are opposites," Mia says with a smile.

Wyatt looks at the ladder. He puts one hand on a rail. Then the other hand. He takes a step up. Then one more. His knees feel a little weak. Mia waits at the bottom. "You can do it," she says. Wyatt climbs up some more. Now he is at the top!

He sits down on the slide. He takes a big breath. Whoosh! He goes down, down, down. His tummy tickles. He lands in the soft sand. "I did it!" Wyatt says. Mia claps her hands. Then they build a little hill in the sand together. Wyatt slides his hand down the small hill. "Fast," he says. He climbs up again for another turn.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: When a grown-up cuts an onion, it can make their eyes sting and water.
story:
Alice wants to make soup for dinner. She wants to make it all by herself. "I will be the cook," she says. Dad will help a little bit.

First, Dad fills the big pot with water. Alice drops in three carrots. Plop, plop, plop. She adds a potato shaped like a square. "A square potato," says Alice. "How funny." Dad laughs too.

Then Dad cuts the onion. He cuts it into little bits. Suddenly Dad's eyes water. Tears run down his face. Alice stops. "Dad, are you sad?" she asks. "Do you need a hug?" Dad wipes his eyes. "No, no," he says. "The onion makes my eyes sting. Onions can do that. Watch." He cuts one more bit, and his eyes water again.

Alice giggles. "Dad is crying onion tears," she says. "Onion tears, onion tears!" She brings him a towel for his face. Then she stirs the soup from her safe spot, far from the hot pot. Dad lifts her up so she can see. The soup bubbles. It smells warm and good.

At dinner, Mom takes one bite. "Mmm," says Mom. "Who made this?" Alice puffs up tall. "The cook did. But the onion made Dad cry first." Dad winks and pretends to cry again. Alice laughs so hard that milk almost comes out of her nose. Then she gives the soup one more stir with her big spoon, like a real cook.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Families pack clothes that fit the weather where they are going, like a swimsuit for the beach or a warm coat for the snow.
story:
Nathan stood on the ferry with his big brother, Sam. The water went splash, splash against the boat. Nathan held his little blue bag. "One bag for me," he said. "Two bags for Sam. Three bags for Mama." Mama counted the bags too.

Nathan opened his bag. He pulled out his swimsuit. "I will swim at the mountain," he said. Sam laughed. "No, Nathan. Look out the window." Nathan looked. The mountains far away were white with snow. Snow, snow, and more snow.

Mama knelt down. "We pack clothes that fit the weather where we are going," she said. "Snowy weather needs warm clothes, not a swimsuit." Nathan put the swimsuit back. He found his black mittens instead. One mitten, two mittens. He put them on. The wool felt soft and warm on his hands.

That night, Nathan had a dream. He dreamed he built a big snowman wearing his very own swimsuit. He laughed in his sleep. In the morning, the ferry blew its loud horn. "To the snow!" Nathan shouted, waving his black mittens out over the rails.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: Apples, bread and carrots are all foods.
story:
Leon was playing store on the kitchen floor. His toys sat in one big line. His teddy bear was the first shopper. "I want to buy things," said Bear, in a growly voice.

Mom gave Leon a basket of things from the kitchen. Inside were an apple, some bread, and one fresh carrot. Leon picked up the carrot. He put it with the toy cars. "Cars do not eat carrots," said Bear. Leon giggled and put the carrot next to the apple. Then the bread went there too.

"Apples, bread and carrots are all foods," said Bear. Leon clapped. Bear paid with a shiny button. Then Bear bit the carrot, and juice went drip, drip, drip all over the floor. "Bear!" laughed Leon. "You made a carrot river!" He grabbed a towel and followed the drip all the way to the rug.

activity: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
knowledge_domain: getting a first library card and borrowing a book
fact: Library books are shared with many other people, so we take care not to tear or write in them.
story:
Lea sat on the city bus next to her mom. She held her new library card in both hands. It had her name on it. On her lap was a book about a big orange cat.

The bus went bump, bump, down the street. Lea felt the seat shake under her. She found a crayon in her pocket. She put the crayon point on the cat page. She wanted to give the cat snowy white whiskers.

Her mom saw the crayon. "Wait," said Mom. "That book belongs to the library. Many other kids share it too. We take care not to draw in it or tear it." Lea pulled the crayon back fast. She looked at the cat. Other kids would want to see those pages too.

Mom pulled some paper from her bag. Lea drew her own cat on the paper. She gave it snowy whiskers and a big smile. The bus went bump, bump, and Lea kept drawing.

At their stop, Mom took Lea's hand. Lea carried the library book under her arm, nice and safe. "Home now," said Mom. Lea said, "Bye bye, bus. Bye bye, cat."

activity: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
knowledge_domain: the five senses and the body parts used for seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting and touching
fact: Glasses help some people see more clearly.
story:
Rose wanted Grandpa to read her book. But the sky was cloudy, so the room was dim. "I can't see the words," Grandpa said. He put on his glasses. Then he could read. Rose wanted to see the glasses too.

She touched them with her fingers. They felt cool and smooth. She heard a little click when they closed. Grandpa let her look. "Do they help you see?" he asked. Rose put them on. The book looked big and funny. "No," she said. "My eyes see fine." Grandpa laughed softly.

He took the glasses back. He read the story. Rose smelled cookies in the oven. Mom brought one over. Rose tasted the sweet cookie. She touched the warm plate. "Read it again," said Rose. Grandpa smiled and turned the page.

activity: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
knowledge_domain: simple object categories such as animals, toys and foods
fact: A toy dog is a toy, not an animal, because it is not alive.
story:
Felix went to the library with his grandma. The librarian had set out big mats and three boxes. One box had a picture of animals. One box had a picture of toys. One box had a picture of foods. "Can you sort these for me?" the librarian asked. Felix nodded his head yes.

He picked up a card with an apple on it. Apples are food. He put it in the food box. He picked up a card with a bear on it. A bear is an animal. It went in the animal box. Then he found a card with a little black dog on it. A dog is an animal, he thought. He put it in the animal box.

Then he looked again. The dog was soft and stuffed. It did not bark. It did not wiggle. It was not alive. "Is this dog a toy?" Felix asked. Grandma smiled. "Look close," she said. Felix held the card up. "Yes, it is a toy," he said. He moved it to the toy box.

"Good sorting," said the librarian. She showed Felix a stamp of a gold star. She pressed it on his hand. Felix laughed and waved the stamp goodbye. "See you next time," he said.

activity: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
knowledge_domain: bringing home a first pet and learning to care for it
fact: A new pet may hide at first while it gets used to its new home.
story:
Charlie got a new bunny. He carried the cage to the backyard. "Hello, bunny!" he said. He opened the cage door. He put out a bowl of water.

The bunny did not hop out. The bunny hid in the back of the cage. Charlie waited. Still the bunny hid. Charlie felt sad. He wanted to pet his bunny so much.

Mom came out with a chair. "Sit here," she said. "The bunny needs time. A new pet hides at first." Charlie sat down. He sat very still. He looked at the clouds. He looked at the flowers.

Then the bunny's nose came out. Then one ear. Then the whole bunny! It hopped into the grass. Charlie giggled. He let the bunny sniff his shoe. "You are safe here," Charlie whispered. Mom took a photo with her phone. Charlie filled the water bowl again, just in case.

activity: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
knowledge_domain: simple safety concepts such as hot versus cold, staying close to caregivers and not touching dangerous objects
fact: At the playground, go down the slide feet first.
story:
Hunter ran into the backyard. He wanted to go down his little slide. The slide sat by the grass. Hunter climbed up the steps. He lay down on his tummy. His head went first. That felt wrong. His tummy did not like it. Hunter turned himself around. Now his feet went first. Down he went, whee, into the soft grass.

Dad was cooking at the grill. Hunter could smell the warm corn. "The grill is hot," said Dad. "I will hold the food. You stay close to me." Hunter stayed by Dad's feet. He did not touch the grill.

After lunch, Hunter built with his red block. He stacked it high. Then he made a messy pile of leaves for his toy truck. The truck went down the leaf pile, feet first, just like Hunter on the slide. Hunter clapped his hands. "Again," he said.

activity: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
knowledge_domain: getting a vaccination shot at the doctor's office
fact: The person giving the shot is the only one who handles the needle; children never touch it.
story:
Sienna sat in the big chair at the doctor's office. Her tummy felt stormy. "I don't like shots," she whispered. "The needle might hurt."

The nurse came in with a little tray. A small needle lay on it. Sienna pointed. "Can I hold the needle? I want to see it."

The nurse smiled. "Only I touch the needle," she said. "That is my job, not yours. But you can hold my sticker sheet."

Sienna took the sticker sheet. It had a flower sticker on top. "I will hold this," she said.

"Good," said the nurse. "Now look at your flower." Sienna looked. The nurse gave the shot so fast. "All done!"

"Wait. That was it?" said Sienna. "It did not hurt much!" She put the flower sticker on her arm.

Afterward, Mom took Sienna to the ice cream shop. Sienna got a pink cone. She licked it and smiled.

The nurse had a needle, and Sienna had a sticker. That was just right.

activity: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
knowledge_domain: pretend play scenarios such as playing house, caring for toys and role-playing simple situations
fact: Pretending means acting as if something is real when it is not.
story:
Leo ran to the play corner at school. Mia and Sam were already there. "The floor is a river!" said Mia. She hopped onto a cushion. "This is my rock."

Leo stopped at the edge. He wanted to play house across the river. But how could he cross? He put one foot on the floor. "No!" cried Sam. "You will splash in the water!"

Leo looked around. He saw three cushions. One, two, three. He counted them out loud. "One, two, three!" Then he jumped. One cushion. Two cushions. Three cushions. He made it to the other side.

"You did it!" said Mia. She handed him a doll. "The baby is sick. Can you help?"

Leo patted the doll. He wrapped her in a small blanket. "My sister does this at home," he said. "She rocks the baby so soft."

"It is not a real baby," said Sam. "We are just pretending. But we act like it is real!"

"Yes!" said Leo. He took his turn to rock the doll. He sang a little song.

Then Mia said, "Time to cook dinner!" She turned a pretend knob on the toy stove. Leo clapped. "Dinner on a rock in a river!" he said. "Best house ever!"

activity: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
knowledge_domain: to hold a pencil correctly and write the letters of their own first name
fact: Some letters are made of straight lines, like L, and some have curves, like O.
story:
James ran into the writing club with his pet turtle in a little box. "Today I write my name!" he said.

Miss Amy gave him a fat pencil. She showed him how to hold it. "Pinch it near the point," she said. James squeezed tight and made a big J. Then a big A. Then an M. He stopped and stared. "Some letters are all straight lines!" The M looked like little sticks.

Miss Amy smiled. "Some letters have curves, like O." James looked at the S in his name. It had curves too, like a little snake. He picked up the curvy letters and made a pile. The straight ones got their own pile. His table was full of letters!

He wrote his name one more time. "Look!" he said. His teacher clapped. James held up the paper so his turtle could see it too.

activity: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
knowledge_domain: to wash their hands with soap for twenty seconds before eating and after the toilet
fact: Drying your hands with a clean towel is the last step of handwashing.
story: Kayden ran to the kitchen. Lunch was on the table. But first, his hands needed a wash. "Soap, water, rub," said Mama. Kayden counted, "One, two, three." He kept rubbing the soap. "Ten, eleven, twelve." Bubbles grew on his hands. "Nineteen, twenty!" Kayden pulled his hands out of the sink. The water did not stop there. It went drip, drip, drip. A drop would fall on his shirt. A drop would fall on the floor. "Where do the drips go?" Kayden wondered. He shook his hands. More drips fell! Then he saw it. A soft white towel hung by the sink. Kayden dried one hand. Then he dried the other hand. All the drips went away. His hands were clean and dry. "Last step," said Kayden. Then he sat down and took a big bite of lunch.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Weeds are plants growing where the gardener does not want them.
story:
Wyatt dug a little hole in the dirt. He dropped in a carrot seed. Mom helped him pat the soil down straight and flat. Every day he came back with his spoon and gave the seed a tiny drink of water.

One morning, green leaves popped up. Wyatt smiled wide. But then he saw more green leaves, in a spot where he had not planted anything. Hmm, he thought. What is this little plant doing here?

He grabbed the funny plant and pulled. "Wait," said Mom. She held his hand. "That one is a carrot. It grows where we planted it. The other one grows where we do not want it. That one is called a weed." Wyatt looked at both plants. One grew in his hole. One grew on the path. He let go of the carrot. He pulled the weed instead, all by himself.

Weeks later, Mom dug up a big orange carrot. She washed it at the sink. Wyatt took a bite and chewed happily. "It grew from my seed," he said. "It grew in the right spot!"

activity: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
knowledge_domain: basic shape concepts such as circle, square, triangle and rectangle
fact: A square turned so a corner points up is still a square.
story:
Lillian wanted to build a house for her toy snake. She looked in the block box. She found a circle block. It rolled away. She found a triangle block. It had three pointy sides. She found a rectangle block. It was long and flat. Then she found a square block. It was just right for the roof.

Her brother Ben ran in. "That's a new shape," he said. He had turned the square block. Now one corner pointed up. Lillian gasped. "My square is gone!" She turned the block back. The flat side was down again. It was the same square! Ben laughed. "You found it, Lillian!"

Lillian put the square on top of the snake house. The snake fit inside. "Silly snake," Lillian said. She picked up a red crayon to color a door. She drew a rectangle door. Then she turned the whole picture. "Look, Ben! My door is still a rectangle!" Ben clapped his hands. "Let's build one more house," he said. Lillian grabbed the square block and shouted, "Yes! The best roof ever!"
